questions.question: A ball thrown straight up has v = 0 at the top. Does gravity stop acting there? Explain the distinction the question tests.
questions.solution: No — at the top the velocity is momentarily zero but the ACCELERATION is still g downward (that is exactly why the ball doesn't stay up). Velocity is the state of motion; acceleration is the rate of change of that state. Zero v with nonzero a is the classic signature of a turning point.

questions.question: What does the area under a velocity–time graph give, and what does its slope give? Apply both to a v–t graph that rises then flattens.
questions.solution: Slope = acceleration; area = displacement (v·dt accumulates distance). Rising then flat: acceleration is positive then zero — the object speeds up then moves at constant velocity, while displacement keeps growing throughout (area keeps accumulating even when v is constant).

questions.question: A feather and a stone dropped in vacuum land together. Why does everyday experience contradict this, and what does the contradiction expose?
questions.solution: In vacuum both have the same acceleration g because a = F/m = mg/m — mass cancels. In air the feather's large area-to-weight ratio makes air resistance comparable to its weight, so its net acceleration is much less. The contradiction exposes air resistance, not a flaw in free-fall theory.

questions.question: Two trains move at 20 m/s and 25 m/s in the same direction. With what velocity does the second approach the first? What if they move oppositely?
questions.solution: Same direction: relative velocity = 25 − 20 = 5 m/s (the gap closes slowly). Opposite directions: 25 + 20 = 45 m/s (rapid closing). Relative velocity is velocity measured in the other object's frame — subtract vectors, which for collinear motion means signed subtraction.

questions.question: Why does a horizontally thrown ball and a ball simply dropped from the same height land at the same time?
questions.solution: Vertical and horizontal motions are independent: gravity acts only vertically, and the horizontal velocity has no vertical component to affect it. Both balls start with zero vertical velocity and fall with the same g — equal fall times, regardless of horizontal speed. Independence of perpendicular components is the heart of projectile motion.
